attempts.raw_response: The debate highlighted a growing tension between traditional journalistic conventions and modern sensibilities regarding gender equality. Critics argued that titles like "Sir" or "Madam" were unnecessary markers of status that perpetuated outdated hierarchies within the newsroom. Supporters, however, maintained that such forms of address were merely polite formalities devoid of malicious intent, reflecting respect for professional achievement rather than gender bias. As digital media platforms increasingly flattened editorial structures, the relevance of these historical prefixes came under intense scrutiny. Readers began to question whether maintaining such distinctions served any purpose beyond reinforcing archaic social norms. The newspaper’s decision to drop the preface was seen as a symbolic gesture toward inclusivity, aiming to create a more welcoming environment for all contributors regardless of their gender identity.

pair.human_continuation: She ended: "Please bring your paper into the modern era and join the ranks of other papers which have removed such a ridiculous and offensive tradition." Responding, Mr Bradshaw said he "had not appreciated that it was causing offence" and the paper, which was founded in 1885, was merely sticking to convention, "as have the [Daily] Telegraph and Private Eye". He added that the use of "Sir" always seemed appropriate, "especially as I am male!". He said many of the letters received were from "regular contributors" who would know who they were addressing. But he added: "In the interests of causing as little offence as possible, from next week we will drop 'Sir' and I would ask others readers to please note this."

In Friday's letter section Ms Hatch, of Henley, wrote: "While I am by no means a feminist, I can't believe it is necessary to maintain such a practice when other papers have eradicated this sexist attitude." She argued that readers of the newspaper probably did not know the gender of the editor and questioned whether it was relevant.
